analysis.one_liner: Requires every U.S. employer to check every worker's eligibility through the federal E-Verify database.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 22 Republican cosponsors but never received a committee vote or any floor action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make E-Verify — a federal database employers use to check whether a worker is authorized to work in the U.S. — mandatory for every employer in the country, and would fund the program permanently. Employers who skip it or keep employing a worker the system flags would face much higher fines, possible criminal charges, and a ban on federal contracts. The bill also directs several agencies, including the Social Security Administration and the IRS, to share records to help find unauthorized workers, and creates a new ICE office to audit employers' hiring paperwork.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose identity documents are being used by someone else, since the bill adds tools to detect multiple uses of the same identity; authorized workers in labor markets where unauthorized competition holds wages down; and the enforcement agencies themselves, which gain new audit, data-sharing, and penalty powers. The bill's sponsor and cosponsors framed it as protecting legal workers by shrinking the market for unauthorized labor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Identity theft victims and enforcement agencies

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires all employers, all federal contractors, and any 'critical' national-security employers to run every new hire — and any current employee never previously checked — through E-Verify, and permanently reauthorizes the program [S2] [S3].

It directs federal agencies to develop algorithms to detect identity theft, such as the same documents or identifying information being used by multiple people, and audits documents submitted to employers [S3].

Civil fines for paperwork violations rise from $100–$1,000 to $1,000–$25,000, hiring fines rise to $2,500–$25,000, repeat violators can be barred from federal contracts for five years, and pattern-of-violations cases can bring prison time of 1–10 years [S3].

Weekly reports on workers who receive a final nonconfirmation go to ICE for enforcement, and a new Employer Compliance Inspection Center within ICE consolidates worksite audits and investigates tax, Social Security, and wage-and-hour violations [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Unauthorized workers already living and working in the U.S. would lose the ability to hold most jobs and lose their income, without any legal-status pathway in the bill. Authorized workers who are wrongly flagged by the system would be fired on the spot if the error becomes final. Small businesses and industries that depend on immigrant labor — agriculture, food processing, construction, hospitality — would face compliance costs, hiring delays, and higher labor costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires employers to immediately terminate any worker who receives a final nonconfirmation, and to treat failure to participate as a violation of immigration law with a presumption of guilt [S3]. E-Verify's underlying government databases contain errors, so authorized U.S. workers can be flagged and would lose their paycheck while contesting the finding — the burden of fixing a government error falls on the worker, not the government.

The bill requires the Social Security Administration, IRS, Treasury, and DHS to build a joint information-sharing program using records including 'no-match' letters and the earnings suspense file — a file of wages reported to the government that didn't match a known name or number — expanding how much employment data agencies cross-check against each other [S3].

Compliance falls hardest on small employers: every hire must be checked within three days, contract and subcontract labor must carry E-Verify certifications or the employer is presumed in violation, and the bill's relief is limited to a demonstration program helping rural small businesses without internet access verify hires at public terminals [S3].

The bill preempts state and local rules restricting E-Verify use and shields employers from liability for firing workers in good-faith reliance on the system, which shifts risk away from employers and onto workers in disputed cases [S3].
The bill contains no provision letting long-residing unauthorized workers legalize their status, so its main effect on that population is job loss rather than a path to documented work [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would genuinely tighten enforcement against employers who hire unauthorized workers, ending a voluntary system where most employers could simply opt out, and its identity-theft provisions address a real harm to legal workers whose numbers are misused. But its design puts the risk of government database errors on workers themselves — immediate termination on a final nonconfirmation, with the presumption of guilt on the employer who skips verification — and it raises labor costs and compliance burdens for small businesses without addressing what happens to workers displaced from the formal economy. It is a strict enforcement bill, not a balanced overhaul of the employment-verification system.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees, then sent to the Judiciary Committee's immigration subcommittee, and stayed there with no committee vote, no markup, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mo Brooks (R-AL) introduced the bill on February 27, 2019, with 16 original cosponsors, all Republicans [S3].
It was referred to the Judiciary, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 8, 2019, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Immigration and Citizenship — the last recorded action [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with 22 cosponsors, all House Republicans [S4].
No committee or subcommittee vote, markup, or floor action ever took place before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, employers who rely on unauthorized labor — agriculture, food processing, construction, hospitality, and staffing agencies — avoided a universal verification mandate and sharply higher penalties, and unauthorized workers kept their ability to work in the formal economy. Small businesses also avoided new compliance costs and database-related firing risk.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled House committees never moved the bill.

industries.note: These industries employ a large share of unauthorized workers and would face labor shortages and sharply higher labor costs under a universal E-Verify mandate with fines up to $25,000 per violation. Their interest in keeping cheap, off-the-books labor available runs against enforcement — and against the wages of legal workers who compete with it.

The bill requires any employer using contract labor to certify in the contract that all parties use E-Verify, or be presumed in violation, putting temp and staffing firms directly in the verification chain.

Every hire must be verified within three days and paperwork violations carry fines up to $25,000, a real compliance burden for small employers. The bill partially offsets this with a DHS demonstration program helping rural small businesses without internet access verify hires at public terminals.

Mandatory, permanently funded E-Verify makes the verification system — including the private services that help employers run checks — a permanent gatekeeper every hire in America must pass through, while the bill simultaneously imposes new audit and fraud-detection duties on the system.
